chapter: Technique, jam sessions, audiences and records
title: Black and White dancers' tastes in music
summary: Smith says he played for either Black or White dances, never mixed; White crowds liked waltzes while Black crowds wanted a beat and blues, except at formal invitation dances.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: One thing that interests me. When you were going around, for instance, with the Blue Devils, at about that time, and you played Black and White dances -- I mean, you played either the Black or White. You didn't play mixed, did you?
Was there much difference in the dancing between the White dancers and the Black dancers?
Back in them days there wasn't much difference. The White people went for waltzes, more so than any other type of music -- for rhythm and time. But Negroes, they didn't care too much for it.
They liked anything that had a...

Yeah, a beat to it. And the Blues and stuff like that. Anything in that (?) stuff, they didn't like that. But as far as waltzes and rhumbas and things like that, they didn't care too much for it, unless it was one of those invitation dances, the Friars or something like that, they called us up -- the big shots. Then it would be all full dress, long skirts...
Right, the (?) classy. What they called a dicty function.
Yeah, that's right. Now, they'd go for it. They'd want you to play that. They don't want too many blues.
